etymologies.etymologyHTML: From earlier hugge (“to embrace, clasp with the arms”) (1560), probably representing a conflation of huck (“to crouch, huddle down”) and Old Norse hugga (“to comfort, console”), from hugr (“mind, heart, thought”), from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“mind, thought, sense”), cognate with Icelandic hugga (“to comfort”), Old English hyġe (“thought”) (whence high (Etymology 2)).

definitions.definition: A close embrace, especially when charged with an emotion such as affection, joy, relief, lust, anger, aggression, compassion, and the like, as opposed to being characterized by formality, equivocation or ambivalence (a half-embrace or "little hug").
(intransitive, obsolete) To crouch; to huddle as with cold.

quote.citation: 1885, M. Quad, Field, Fort and Fleet, page 354:
quote.text: They had a slight breast work, and they hugged down behind it and waited.

quote.citation: 1892, Paul Boyton, The Story of Paul Boyton:
quote.text: That is why they are so little known and never explored. During the day, when a Chilean cruiser nosed around uncomfortably close, the little sloop would be hugged under the lee of one of the islands, sail lowered and anchor dropped.
bright rocks whose stain of emerald or quartz shaft of shine the starfish hugged beneath the tide .
She put her feet on a rung and hugged down against her knees, making herself even smaller.
Zhai Tingshen stood at the window upstairs, his black eyes staring intently at the figure that was tightly hugged below.

definitions.definition: (transitive or reciprocal) To embrace by holding closely, especially in the arms.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VIII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: We toted in the wood and got the fire going nice and comfortable. Lord James still set in one of the chairs and Applegate had cabbaged the other and was hugging the stove.

quote.citation: 2020 October 21, Dr Joseph Brennan, “From the main line and over the waves”, in Rail, page 60:
quote.text: Gourock also boasted a pier railway, although its pier hugged the shore rather than jutting into the bay.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figurative) To hold fast; to cling to; to cherish.

quote.citation: 1665, Joseph Glanvill, Scepsis Scientifica: Or, Confest Ignorance, the Way to Science; […], London:  […]  E. C[otes] for Henry Eversden […], →OCLC:
quote.text: We hug intellectual deformities, if they bear our names
